content:
Your home just took a hit from a storm, and now a second worry sets in right behind the first one. Will insurance actually cover this, or are you about to pay for the damage yourself.

We have worked alongside homeowners through this exact moment more times than we can count. Here is what typically gets covered, what does not, and how to make sure your claim gets approved instead of denied.

What Homeowners Insurance Usually Covers

Most standard homeowners insurance policies cover storm damage caused by wind, hail, and fallen trees, as long as the damage is sudden and accidental rather than the result of long term neglect.

This typically includes roof damage from wind or falling debris, water damage that enters through a storm created opening, and structural damage from a tree or large branch falling on the home. The key word in every policy is sudden. Damage that built up slowly over months, like a roof leak nobody addressed, is treated very differently than damage from a single storm event.

What Often Gets Excluded or Disputed

Not every type of storm related damage gets an automatic approval, and this is where many homeowners run into trouble.

Flood Damage Requires Separate Coverage

Standard homeowners insurance typically does not cover flood damage from rising water. This requires a separate flood insurance policy, which surprises many homeowners after the fact.

Pre Existing Damage Gets Scrutinized

If an adjuster believes damage existed before the storm, or resulted from a lack of maintenance, the claim can be reduced or denied entirely. This is why documentation matters so much before repairs begin.

Wind Versus Flood Disputes

In coastal areas, insurers sometimes argue that damage was caused by flooding rather than wind, since flood damage often falls under a separate policy. This distinction alone causes a significant number of claim disputes every storm season.

How to Strengthen Your Claim Before an Adjuster Arrives

The steps you take in the first hours after storm damage directly affect whether your claim moves smoothly or gets delayed.

  • Photograph all damage from multiple angles before any cleanup begins
  • Keep receipts for any emergency repairs, such as tarping or board up work
  • Avoid throwing away damaged materials until the adjuster has reviewed them
  • Request a written damage assessment from a licensed restoration contractor
  • Keep a written log of every call made and every name spoken with

An adjuster working from thorough documentation approves claims faster than one working from a verbal description alone.

A Real Claim, Start to Finish

A homeowner in Tampa filed a claim after storm damage tore off a section of roofing and allowed water into an upstairs bedroom. The initial adjuster visit undervalued the damage, missing structural issues hidden beneath the visible roof damage.

Our team had already documented the full scope of the damage before the adjuster's first visit, including photos of the structural framing exposed by the storm. This documentation gave the homeowner grounds to request a reassessment, and the claim was ultimately approved for the full scope of repair, not just the initial partial estimate.

Why Documentation Timing Matters So Much

I always advise clients to document everything before any repair work begins, not after. Once cleanup starts, the evidence an adjuster needs to approve a fair settlement often disappears along with the debris.

I prioritize a strategy where our team assesses and photographs storm damage the same way an insurance adjuster would, before the adjuster even schedules their visit. This puts homeowners in a stronger position from the very first conversation with their insurance company.

How We Support Homeowners Through the Claims Process

Our insurance claim assistance service exists specifically to close the gap between what happened to your home and what your policy actually covers. Filing a claim alone, without professional documentation, often leads to a lower settlement than the damage actually warrants.

If a tree fell on your home during the storm, our earlier guide on what to do in the first 24 hours after a tree falls on your roof covers the immediate safety steps to take before documentation even begins.

Final Thoughts

Homeowners insurance typically covers sudden storm damage from wind, hail, and fallen trees, but flood damage and disputed pre existing conditions often complicate a claim. Document everything before cleanup starts, and get a professional damage assessment early to protect the full value of your claim.

faqs.q: Does homeowners insurance cover a tree falling on my roof?
faqs.a: In most cases, yes, since this is typically classified as sudden storm damage rather than gradual wear.

faqs.q: Is flood damage covered under standard homeowners insurance?
faqs.a: No. Flood damage usually requires a separate flood insurance policy and is not covered under a standard homeowners policy.

faqs.q: What should I do before an insurance adjuster arrives?
faqs.a: Photograph all damage, avoid discarding damaged materials, and request a professional damage assessment before any cleanup begins.

faqs.q: Can a contractor help with my insurance claim directly?
faqs.a: Yes. A licensed restoration contractor can document damage and provide assessments that support your claim during the adjuster review process.

faqs.q: Why do some storm damage claims get denied?
faqs.a: Claims are often denied or reduced due to disputes over pre existing damage, missing documentation, or confusion between wind and flood related causes.
